Content:
Suppose we have a finite population of size [MATH: N] in which a proportion [MATH: p] of individuals has a particular characteristic.

Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw that we can estimate the sampling distribution of [MATH: p] as

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right)]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion,
- [MATH: N] is the population size, and
- [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Content:
Recall that the quantity
[MATH: \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}]
is the finite population correction factor applied to the variance of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.] It is appropriate to apply this correction factor whenever [MATH: n > 5\%\cdot N.]

Content:
Now, recall that the [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for [MATH: p] in the cases where [MATH: n > 5\%\cdot N] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm \overbrace{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} }}^{\textrm{margin of error}}]

Content:
where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1).]

Content:
Suppose we require the margin of error to be smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon.] Then, we must have

Content:
[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} } \leq \varepsilon]

Content:
By isolating [MATH: n,] we can find the minimum sample size needed for the margin or error to be smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon.] We learned how to do this for large populations in a previous lesson.

Content:
To isolate [MATH: n,] we start by squaring both sides:

Content:
[MATH: z_{\alpha/2}^2 \cdot \dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \leq \varepsilon^2]

Content:
Dividing this inequality by [MATH: \varepsilon^2] and rearranging slightly, we get
[MATH: z_{\alpha/2}^2 \cdot \dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{n(N-1)} \leq 1.]
Now, we let
[MATH: m = z_{\alpha/2}^2 \cdot \dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}.]
Then, our inequality becomes
[MATH: m\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{n(N-1)} \leq 1.]
We can solve for [MATH: n] as follows:
[MATH: m ⋅ (N − n)|≤ n(N − 1); mN − mn|≤ nN − n; mN|≤ mn + nN − n; mN|≤ n(m + N − 1); n|≥ (Nm)/(m + N − 1)]

sections.normalized_html:
Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] for a small population can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm \overbrace{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}}}^{\large \textrm{margin of error}},]

where

  • [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,

  • [MATH: p] is the population proportion,

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: N] is the population size satisfying the condition [MATH: n > 0.05\cdot N,]

  • [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

If we require the margin of error to be at most [MATH: \varepsilon,] then

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}} \leq \varepsilon.]

Doing some algebra to isolate [MATH: n,] we get [MATH: n \geq \dfrac{Nm}{N + m - 1},] where [MATH: m = \dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}] is the minimum sample size needed when the population is large.

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.99=0.01 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.005.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 2.576) = 0.005.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.005} = 2.576.]

We're given the estimate [MATH: \widehat{\,p} = 10\% = 0.1.] Therefore, substituting

[MATH: \varepsilon=0.02, \qquad \widehat{\,p}=0.1, \qquad z_{\alpha/2}=2.576] into the inequality for [MATH: n,] we obtain

[MATH: m|= (z_{α/2}^{2}p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(ε^{2}); = ((2.576)^{2}0.1(1 − 0.1))/((0.02)^{2}); ≈ 1493.05,; n|≥ (Nm)/(N + m − 1); = (630 ⋅ 1493.05)/(630 + 1493.05 − 1); ≈ 443.26.]

Finally, rounding up to the nearest integer, we get that [MATH: n=444] or larger.

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] for a small population can be written as

where

- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion,
- [MATH: n] is the sample size,
- [MATH: N] is the population size satisfying the condition [MATH: n > 0.05\cdot N,]
- [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

If we require the margin of error to be at most [MATH: \varepsilon,] then

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1}} \leq \varepsilon.]

Doing some algebra to isolate [MATH: n,] we get
[MATH: n \geq \dfrac{Nm}{N + m - 1},]
where
[MATH: m = \dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{\varepsilon^2}]
is the minimum sample size needed when the population is large.

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.99=0.01 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.005.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 2.576) = 0.005.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.005} = 2.576.]

We're given the estimate [MATH: \widehat{\,p} = 10\% = 0.1.] Therefore, substituting

[MATH: \varepsilon=0.02, \qquad

[MATH: m|= (z_{α/2}^{2}p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(ε^{2}); = ((2.576)^{2}0.1(1 − 0.1))/((0.02)^{2}); ≈ 1493.05,; n|≥ (Nm)/(N + m − 1); = (630 ⋅ 1493.05)/(630 + 1493.05 − 1); ≈ 443.26.]
